title: The Laplace Transform
intro: The Laplace transform turns a signal x(t) into a function X(s) on the complex plane. This topic reads it as a landscape: a surface standing over the s-plane, held up by poles, pinned down by zeros, and cut along the imaginary axis to give the frequency response.

blocks.text: A continuous-time signal is a function $x(t)$ of time. The Laplace transform packs all of it into a single function of a complex variable $s$:

Every value of $s = \sigma + j\omega$ is a point in the complex plane, so $X(s)$ gives a complex number at every point. Its size $|X(s)|$ is a height, and plotting that height above the plane gives a surface. Almost everything about the Laplace transform can be read off that surface:

items: Poles are where the surface shoots up to infinity, like tent poles holding up a canvas.
Zeros are where it touches the floor, $X(s) = 0$.

The region of convergence (ROC) is the part of the plane where the integral actually comes to a finite number. It is always a vertical strip: everything right of a line, left of a line, or between two lines.
The imaginary axis $s = j\omega$ is where the Laplace transform becomes the Fourier transform. Walking up the axis and reading the height gives how strongly each frequency passes.
Whether a system is stable or causal is a question about where the ROC sits relative to the imaginary axis and the poles.

blocks.text: The z-transform of discrete-time signals is the same idea with circles in place of vertical lines; the library's topic The Z-Transform (#/math/z-transform) has the matching viewer, and the Gallery of Signals (#/math/laplace-transform/gallery) page shows how the two planes map onto each other.

The viewer below draws that surface for eleven input signals. Pick one from Input signal, then press Next step ▶ to walk through it in eight steps: the signal, the integral, the poles and zeros, the surface, the ROC, the imaginary axis, reading the height with a ruler, and stability and causality. The panel that each step is about is outlined.

items: Drag the 3D view to turn it, or use Turn and Tilt. A tilt near 85° looks straight down and turns the surface into a contour map of the pole-zero plot.
Decay rate a and Frequency ω₀ move the poles and zeros of the signals that use them (the readout says when a signal ignores one). A negative a makes a signal grow instead of decay.

Probe frequency ω moves the red point up the imaginary axis. The s-plane panel draws a green line from every zero and a dashed violet line from every pole to it; the response panel marks the same frequency. Sweep ω moves it for you.
Height shows switches between decibels, $20\log_{10}|X(s)|$, which makes zeros into deep pits and keeps poles in view, and the plain magnitude $|X(s)|$, which shows how sharp a resonance really is.
Solid colour is inside the ROC, faded colour outside it. The shaded strip in the s-plane panel is the ROC from above.

blocks.text: The surface in decibels is clipped at +30 dB and −30 dB, so a pole appears as a flat plateau and a zero as a flat-bottomed pit. Mathematically the pole goes to infinity and the zero to minus infinity in decibels. The view covers σ and ω from −3 to 3.

items: Points of the s-Plane (#/math/laplace-transform/s-plane): what $e^{-st}$ does to a signal, as a turning arrow that grows or shrinks, and why some vertical lines make the integral converge.
The Surface |X(s)| (#/math/laplace-transform/surface): factoring $X(s)$ into poles and zeros, and why that fixes the whole landscape.
The Region of Convergence (#/math/laplace-transform/region-of-convergence): strips and half-planes, right-sided and left-sided signals, and two signals with the same formula.
The Imaginary Axis and Frequency Response (#/math/laplace-transform/imaginary-axis): slicing the surface along $s = j\omega$, and reading the response with a ruler.
Pole Positions and the Time Signal (#/math/laplace-transform/poles-and-time): how far left a pole sits sets the decay, its height sets the oscillation, and stability follows.
Properties of the Transform (#/math/laplace-transform/properties): delay, shifts in s, scaling, differentiation, integration and convolution, and the initial and final value theorems.

Solving Differential Equations (#/math/laplace-transform/differential-equations): the reason engineers learn this transform: derivatives become multiplication by $s$, and a circuit or a spring becomes algebra.
Inverting the Transform (#/math/laplace-transform/inverse): getting $x(t)$ back, by partial fractions or by integrating up a line in the ROC.
A Gallery of Signals (#/math/laplace-transform/gallery): every signal in the viewer, walked through from time signal to stability, and the bridge to the z-plane.

blocks.text: Complex numbers in polar form, $e^{j\theta} = \cos\theta + j\sin\theta$, and the integral of an exponential, $\int_0^\infty e^{-ct}\,dt = 1/c$ when the real part of $c$ is positive. This topic writes the imaginary unit as $j$, as engineers do; mathematicians write $i$. The library's page Complex Numbers (#/quantum/foundations/complex-numbers) covers the polar form, and Integrals (#/math/calculus/integrals) covers integration.

Engineers mostly use the one-sided transform, $\int_{0^-}^{\infty}$, because their signals start at a switch-on time. This topic starts from the two-sided integral over all time, so that left-sided and two-sided signals fit in the same picture; for a signal that is zero before $t = 0$ the two agree. The Solving Differential Equations (#/math/laplace-transform/differential-equations) page switches to the one-sided form, where initial conditions come in.
